info.bio:
Alice in Chains es una banda Rock estadounidense, fundada en 1987 en Seattle, Washington. 

Alice in Chains se formó oficialmente cuando el cantante Layne Staley y el guitarrista Jerry Cantrell se conocieron en una fiesta y decidieron formar una banda, ya que compartían gustos musicales y habían estado tocando en bandas de glam metal(Jerry Cantrell en Diamond Dave), estilo predominante en la época. Poco después se uniría al grupo el bajista Mike Starr (bajista del grupo de Glam Gyspy Rose) y el batería Sean Kinney

scenes.name: Grunge
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …styles that involved "hard" vibrations. Those were the four cardinal points of Seattle's grunge. Nirvana had turned grunge into a slot machine. podcast.title: Early Days (1991)
podcast.body: During the filming of *Singles* in early 1991, Alice in Chains was still in its early stages, primarily "trying to be a glimy hair metal band." This indicates their musical evolution was ongoing and predated their full embrace of the grunge sound that would later define them and the Seattle scene. "Allison James was still trying to be a glimy hair metal band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Escalating Addiction and Financial Loss (Post-1991)
podcast.body: As Alice in Chains gained popularity, Layne Staley's increased wealth fueled his intensifying drug habit, which reached a tipping point after 1991. By the mid-90s, his condition was very poor. His addiction caused Alice in Chains to lose substantial income because they couldn't be booked for tours, including bailing as the opener for a Metallica tour in 1994, as Staley was too strung out. "Allison Chains lost tons and tons of money because they just couldn't be booked for tours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cameo in Singles (1992)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains made a cameo appearance in the 1992 Hollywood motion picture *Singles*. The film was significant for not only featuring the music of the moment but also including appearances from prominent bands and figures of the burgeoning alternative and grunge scene, helping to expand grunge's reach. "It was a Hollywood motion picture that not only featured the music of the moment, but also cameos from Pearl Jam and Chris Cornell and Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singles Soundtrack Contribution (1992)
podcast.body: Songs from Alice in Chains were widely played on the radio and in alternative clubs throughout late 1992, following the release of *Singles*. The movie and its soundtrack were instrumental in expanding the reach and popularity of grunge music. "Songs from Allison Chains, Pearl Jam, The Screaming Trees and The Smashing Pumpkins were all played on the radio and in alternative clubs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Girlfriend's Death and Isolation (1996)
podcast.body: In October 1996, Layne Staley's long-term girlfriend, Demri Parrott, died from a bacterial infection she contracted due to her own drug abuse, which settled in her heart's lining. After her death, Staley became a recluse in his penthouse condo, spending his time painting, playing video games, watching TV, and having heroin and cocaine ("his medicine") delivered by a network of dealers. He ceased rehab attempts and became increasingly isolated. "Lane's longtime girlfriend, Demir Parrott, died. As the result of a bacterial infection, she picked up as the result of her own drug abuse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Breakup Due to Frontman's Inactivity (November 1997)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains officially broke up in November 1997 because of frontman Layne Staley's severe drug problems and subsequent inactivity. Staley's deteriorating health and isolation made it impossible for the band to continue. "With nothing happening with their frontman, Allison Chains broke up in November 1997."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Management Company and Alias (April 1997)
podcast.body: The Alice in Chains Management Company, through the "LaRusta Trust," purchased a condo for Layne Staley in Seattle in April 1997. Staley used the alias "John LaRusta" to keep his real name out of public records during this transaction, indicating a desire for privacy even in his living arrangements. "The purchaser was the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Allison Chains Management Company. John LaRusta was an alias used by Lane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording Outfit for Layne Staley (Post-1997)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit in Layne Staley's condo. This was an effort to allow Staley to continue making music, although he reportedly used it only "once in a while," preferring to paint, watch TV, play video games, and do drugs. "Allison Chains guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit that Lane used once in a while, but mostly he just painted, watched TV, played video games, and did drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (2002)
podcast.body: Around March 1992 (likely a transcription error for March 2002), Layne Staley is thought to have contracted an infection; years of drug abuse and malnutrition had severely compromised his immune system. His health deteriorated. On April 19th, 2002, his accountants, noticing no bank activity for two weeks, prompted his mother and stepfather to visit his condo with police. After breaking down the door, they found his body. The coroner estimated his death occurred around April 5th, 2002, coincidentally the eighth anniversary of Kurt Cobain's death. "On April 19th, 2002, his accountants noticed that there hadn't been any activity with his bank account for two weeks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley Death (April 2002) – Speedball Overdose After Years of Reclusion
podcast.body: Vocalist Layne Staley died in 2002 of a speedball overdose (cocaine and heroin) following years of complete self-imposed reclusion and extreme physical deterioration, having reportedly reached a body weight of only 36 kilograms. His body was not discovered until two weeks after his death, and was so severely decomposed that identification took 24 hours. "His body was found two weeks after his death and was so disfigured that it took 24 hours to identify him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley Found Dead April 19, 2002; William DuVall Joined, Three Albums Followed
podcast.body: Layne Staley was the person around whom Alice in Chains was originally formed in 1984. By 1995, heroin had rendered him almost unable to function; the band could neither record nor tour. His body was found on April 19, 2002, in his Seattle condo after two weeks of no contact, still with a syringe in its arm. After a 2004 tsunami benefit with various substitute vocalists, the band decided to continue and eventually settled on William DuVall from a Los Angeles band called Comes with the Fall — who could blend his voice with guitarist Jerry Cantrell's harmonics and was also a capable guitarist. Three Alice in Chains albums followed. "He was also a pretty fair guitar player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Death (2002)
podcast.body: Layne Staley was found dead on April 19, 2002, after his parents called the police when they hadn't heard from him for two weeks. The coroner determined he had died two weeks earlier, on April 5. A needle was still in his arm when he was discovered. "That was April 19th, 2002. The corner said he died two weeks earlier on April 5th. A needle was still hanging from his arm when they found him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Death (Early April 2002)
podcast.body: Staley died sometime in the first week of April 2002, though his body was not found until two weeks later, on April 19. "Lane eventually died. It was sometime in the first week of April of 2002. He wasn't found until two weeks later. It was the 19th one they found him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Death and Discovery (April 5-19, 2002)
podcast.body: Layne Staley died around Friday, April 5, 2002, an anniversary date shared with Kurt Cobain's death. His body was discovered on April 19, 2002, after his mother became concerned. On April 17, she found a pile of uncollected mail outside his condo. Two days later, accountants informed his former manager, Susan Silver, that no money had been withdrawn from his bank account for two weeks. When his mother returned to the condo and heard his usually quiet cat, Sadie, meowing excessively, she called 911. Police broke in and found Staley's body with drug paraphernalia scattered nearby; an autopsy determined he had been dead for approximately two weeks. "The autopsy deterrent that he'd been dead for about two weeks, probably dying on Friday, April 5, the day after Mike Stars visit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 6: (50-41)

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Last Known Interaction (April 4, 2002)
podcast.body: On Thursday, April 4, 2002, former Alice in Chains bandmate Mike Starr visited Layne Staley's condo. Starr was shocked by Staley's severely deteriorated appearance and urged him to call 911, but Staley refused. Starr eventually left, feeling angry, discouraged, and sad, telling Staley, "not like this, don't leave like this." Mike Starr is believed to have been the last person to see Layne Staley alive. "Looks like he was the last guy to see Lane alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 6: (50-41)

podcast.title: Dropped by Label (2004)
podcast.body: After 15 years, Alice in Chains was dropped from their record label in 2004, following Layne Staley's death and years of inactivity. "In 2004, they were dropped from the record label after 15 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami Benefit Catalyst (Boxing Day 2004)
podcast.body: The reunion process began when Jerry Cantrell, Mike Inez, and Sean Kinney were asked to perform at a benefit concert for victims of the Indian Ocean tsunami, agreeing to play with a series of guest singers. "The thing that started the reunion was the Indian Ocean tsunami on Boxing Day 2004."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion for Tsunami Benefit (2005)
podcast.body: In 2005, drummer Sean Kinney initiated the idea of reuniting the band for a benefit concert to aid victims of the tsunami that struck Thailand, Indonesia, and other parts of Southeast Asia. The concert was well-received. "In 2005, drummer Sean Kinney came up with the idea of reuniting the band for a benefit concert for the victims of the tsunami that hit Thailand, Indonesia, and other places in Southeast Asia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: First Gig with William DuVall (September 22, 2006)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains made their first appearance with William DuVall as their vocalist at a gig in Las Vegas on this date. "The first time Alison Chains appeared with DuVall as their vocalist was at a gig in Las Vegas on September the 22nd 2006."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Second Benefit with Guest Vocalists (Spring 2006)
podcast.body: In the spring of 2006, the band played another benefit with guest vocalists, one of whom was William DuVall, who would later become their permanent singer. "In the spring of 2006, they played another benefit again with a series of guest vocalists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Ambassadors for Grunge
podcast.body: With their hit "Man in the Box," Alice in Chains "proved to be ambassadors for the Grunge sound and the Seattle scene" by mid-1991, helping to introduce the new sound to a wider audience. "Man in the Box and Alice in Shains proved to be ambassadors for the Grunge sound and the Seattle scene."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Band in Limbo (Post-Staley's Death)
podcast.body: After Staley's death, Alice in Chains never formally broke up but entered a "land of limbo," essentially ceasing to exist due to the loss of their singer and the profound impact of his death on the members. "Alison Chains never really broke up, but with no singer and so many scars affecting so many members of the band, they really didn't exist either. So they were in this land of limbo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Bridging Rock and Metal
podcast.body: Along with Soundgarden, Nirvana, and Smashing Pumpkins, Alice in Chains contributed to slowly closing the "big attitude gap between rock and old school metal" throughout the early to middle 90s, fostering a new open-mindedness in music. "bands like Soundgarden and Silverchair Nirvana and the smashing pumpkins and Alice and Chains slowly closed that big attitude gap between rock and old school metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collective Achievement Surpassed Solo Work
podcast.body: The band's collective output and accomplishments were of a significantly higher order than Jerry Cantrell's individual solo recordings. "but nothing anywhere near the order of what Allyson accomplished together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comeback and Association with Alternative Metal
podcast.body: Alice in Chains saw renewed success in the 2010s, being explicitly mentioned in the context of Alternative Metal and Alternative Hard Rock, a genre prominent in the 1990s. This comeback was part of a larger trend of older groups returning to the forefront. "And this is where we run into sound garden and outs and chains again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Early 90s Grunge Influence
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was a key band in the grunge movement that gained popularity in late 1991, with their music being extensively consumed by teenagers in that era.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Early Co-Management and Susan Silver's Involvement
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was initially co-managed by Kelly Curtis. When Curtis became distracted by the growing popularity of his other band, Mother Love Bone, Susan Silver took over much of the day-to-day management for Alice in Chains. It was Silver who secured their record deal.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Sound and Image Shift
podcast.body: The original Alice in Chains had a sound more akin to Van Halen and Mötley Crüe than Grunge. However, they underwent a change of image and sound tweaks when the Seattle grunge scene began to emerge, which proved to be a successful move for the band. "The original Allison Chains was more Van Halen and Motley Crude than Grunge. But then, when everybody realized what was going on around them in Seattle, there was a change of image and a couple of sound tweaks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Embraced by Traditional Rock Fans
podcast.body: A distinguishing characteristic of Alice in Chains was their strong appeal to traditional rock fans, even more so than alternative rock fans. Their songs often charted on the Album Rock Chart before making significant headway on the Modern Rock Chart. "They were embraced by traditional rock fans, more than alternative rock fans."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Equal Album Output with New Singer
podcast.body: The version of Alice in Chains featuring William DuVall has released as many full albums as the band did with Layne Staley on vocals. "This version has now released as many full albums with Duval as they had with lane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: First Gold Seattle Album
podcast.body: Their debut album "Facelift" achieved gold status by September 1991, marking it as the first Seattle scene album of the 1990s to reach this sales milestone. "By September, the Facelift album had gone gold, the first 90s Seattle scene album to do so."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Formation and Name Origin
podcast.body: Layne Staley had been living with a homeless Jerry Cantrell at their rehearsal space when Sleeze, Staley's band, was eventually renamed Alice in Chains. After Staley's other band (a funk outfit) and Cantrell's separate project both broke up, Cantrell and Sean Kinney asked Staley to be the vocalist for their new group, adopting the name of Staley's former band, Alice in Chains, for the new project. "Sleeze was eventually renamed Alice in Chains, while Lane was living with a homeless Jerry Cantrell at their rehearsal space."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Founding Members and Early Lineup
podcast.body: Guitarist Jerry Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney were the founders of Alice in Chains. Layne Staley was not a founder; he was drafted in early from a glam band called Sleeze, for whom he played drums. "That was guitarist Jerry Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney. But he was drafted in early from another band, a glam group called Sleeze, for whom he played drums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Global Alt Rock Explosion
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was listed as one of the groups responsible for the global explosion of alt rock attitude in the 1990s, a period where alt rock became predominantly guitar-based. "thanks to groups like Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Sound Guard and Allison Chained and smashing pumpkins and stone-tiple pile with and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge Movement Leader
podcast.body: Alice in Chains (referred to as "Allison Chains") was a key band in the grunge movement, contributing "riff-ready songs" that caused alt-rock to coalesce around hard guitar rock. They were instrumental in the genre's rise to mainstream prominence.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heavy Metal Roots
podcast.body: Alice in Chains distinguished themselves from other Grunge bands with their "more obvious heavy metal roots," aligning with the "doomy end of the metal scene" rather than the punk-metal fusion of Soundgarden. Both Layne Staley and Jerry Cantrell had played in metal bands before forming Alice in Chains in 1987. "What distinguished them was their more obvious heavy metal roots."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Heroin Decimation
podcast.body: Heroin tragically decimated and brought death to the band members of Alice in Chains. "Heroin decimated and brought death to the New York dolls. The pretenders sublime, smashing pumpkins, allyson chains, skinny puppy holes, Scott Wylin, D.D. Ramone, Billy Eidle, a chunk of ever-clear, a vast swath of the Britpop scene of the 1990s, and pretty much everyone who's ever been in the Red Hot Chili Peppers past in present."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence of Grunge on Rock
podcast.body: Alice in Chains, as part of the grunge movement, helped to close the "attitude gap" between rock and old-school metal in the early and mid-90s. The band, along with others like Nirvana and Soundgarden, acknowledged the significant influence of bands such as Black Sabbath, Judas Priest, and Kiss on their music. "Boys like Kurt Cobain and the dudes from Soundguard, Dinales and Chains weren't shy about saying, hey, don't diss black Sabbath and Judas Priest and kiss, they were pretty good bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Zero
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was one of the diverse musical tastes shared among the members of the band Zero, which would later evolve into Linkin Park. "Allison Chains, the Roots, the Prodigy, you mix it all together and it all came out like this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lane Staley's Death – Impact on Susan Silver
podcast.body: The death of Alice in Chains singer Lane Staley was a significant event that occurred during Susan Silver's management tenure and personal relationship with Chris Cornell. This tragic loss was mentioned in the context of the difficulties Silver faced leading up to her divorce from Cornell. "Not to mention the total implosion and death of Allison Chains singer Lane Staley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Continued Tenure Despite Drug Use
podcast.body: The band retained Layne Staley despite his drug problems, keeping him "until he drugged himself to death," highlighting a perceived double standard in how the band handled substance abuse among its members. "yet they kept senior Lane Staley until he drugged himself to death."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Decline and Isolation
podcast.body: Following his girlfriend's overdose death in 1996, Layne Staley's drug hell intensified, and he largely withdrew from the world, living a hermetic existence in a condo. During this period, he spent his time painting, playing video games, and doing drugs, while his physical health rapidly deteriorated. His arms became covered with sores that threatened to become gangrenous, his teeth rotted, and his weight plummeted to around one hundred pounds, as he could only keep down protein drinks. "He lived a hermetic existence in a condo, painting and playing video games and doing drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 6: (50-41)

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Decline and Isolation (Late Original Existence)
podcast.body: In the band's final years of original existence, singer Layne Staley became a "super hard core junkie," largely confined to his condo, painting, playing video games, and injecting smack. He rarely ventured out, had drugs delivered, and lost teeth due to malnutrition. "And this is because senior Lane Staley had turned into such a super hard court junkie, and he wasn't able to do much of anything except staying his condo and paint and play video games and shoot smack into his veins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Drug Addiction and Decline
podcast.body: Around 1995, Layne Staley's drug habit spiraled out of control, leading to his virtual disappearance from 1996 onward. His last performance with the band was on July 3, 1996, in Kansas City, during a tour with KISS. He became a severe addict, barricading himself in his Seattle condo, where he painted, played video games, and had drugs delivered, leaving the band paralyzed. "Lane turned into an irreparable junkie, barricading himself in his Seattle condo where he painted, played video games, and had all his drugs delivered to the door."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Heroin Addiction
podcast.body: Layne Staley, singer for Alice in Chains, began using heroin in the early 1990s. Despite numerous attempts at rehabilitation, he was unable to maintain sobriety. The death of Kurt Cobain in 1994 initially scared him, but he soon returned to his drug use. After his girlfriend died of an overdose in 1996, Staley's addiction worsened, leading him to lose the will to live, become hermetic, and render him unable to tour or record with Alice in Chains. "He started shooting heroin in the early 1990s, and despite several attempts at rehab, nothing stuck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 6: (50-41)

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Inherited Addiction
podcast.body: Layne Staley's father was a heavy drug user, suggesting a family history of addiction. "Lane's father was a heavy drug user, so like father, like son."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Vocal Style
podcast.body: Layne Staley's voice and his harmonies with Jerry Cantrell were central to the band's sound, considered the best hard rock harmonies since David Lee Roth and Michael Anthony in Van Halen's early days. Their vocal arrangements often featured dual lead vocals, strategically overlapped, with the two voices typically separated by a major third. Staley, with the more powerful delivery, could transition from a menacing monotone to sharp, cutting explosions, and also had a great scream, appealing to both metal and alternative fans. "Technically, the two voices were separated by a major third with Lane having the more powerful of the two deliveries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Lewis Carroll-inspired Name
podcast.body: The band's name, Alice in Chains, was described as a "portentous play on Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland," hinting at the dark and surreal themes in their music. "whose name was a portentous play on Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Major Label Signing
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was one of the significant bands from the developing Seattle scene that major record labels actively pursued and successfully signed. They were specifically signed by Columbia Records. "Major record labels had heard about the developing scene and they were in town, snapping up some of the bigger bands. Allison Chains, they were signed by Columbia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Managed by Susan Silver and Kelly Curtis – Early Co-Management
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was initially managed by Susan Silver, Chris Cornell's ex-wife, in partnership with Kelly Curtis. When Curtis shifted his focus to manage Pearl Jam, Silver took on sole management responsibilities for Alice in Chains, navigating the band through challenges including singer Lane Staley's death. "Kelly and his buddy Ken managed Allison Chains. When Mother Lovebone started to get hot, Kelly wanted to spend more time with them. Meanwhile, Ken wanted out, so Susan and Kelly became co-managers of Allison Chains through their own management company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Management and Major Label Deal
podcast.body: Alice in Chains rose alongside Soundgarden in the Seattle scene, sharing managers Kelly Curtis and Susan Silver. They secured a direct major label deal with Columbia Records, bypassing the extensive independent label history that many of their contemporaries experienced. "Music managers Kelly Curtis and Susan Silver, who also oversaw Soundgarden, took on Alice as clients."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Mariah O'Brien's Cover Shoot
podcast.body: Mariah O'Brien, known for appearing on Spinal Tap's "Bitch School" single, posed for the *Dirt* album cover on June 14, 1992. She lay in the body-shaped hole in the studio's "desert" set for eight hours while photographer Rocky Schenk took hundreds of shots and adjusted lighting. O'Brien later recalled having to hold her urge to urinate during the lengthy session. It was clarified that O'Brien, not singer Layne Staley's then-girlfriend Demri Parrott, is the woman on the cover. Today, Mariah O'Brien works as an interior designer in Los Angeles. "Mariah had to lie in that hole for eight hours as Schenk took hundreds of shots, adjusting the lighting countless times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 1

podcast.title: Members' Catalog Sales
podcast.body: Members of Alice in Chains are mentioned among artists who have sold their music catalogs. "members of Allison Chains have cashed out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Metaphorical Lyrical Approach
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was cited as an example of a Grunge band whose lyrics were "framed in metaphors," showcasing a lyrical style that contrasted with the more direct, first-person narratives of later Post-Grunge acts. "Compare how many songs by Nirvana Pro Jam, Alice and Change and Soundgarden used the word I in the lyrics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mike Starr's Bass Playing
podcast.body: Bassist Mike Starr was credited with providing a "cool foundation" for Alice in Chains' sound. "Go back and listen to some of those Allison Chains records and hear how Mike Star provided a cool foundation for everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mike Starr's Dismissal for Drug Use
podcast.body: Mike Starr was dismissed from Alice in Chains for being a "druggie." "Mike Star was let go from Alice and Chains for being a drugie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Participation in Mad Season Project
podcast.body: Despite his severe addiction, Layne Staley managed to participate in the Mad Season project. Mike McCready and John Baker Saunders supported him through the recording sessions, hoping that working with sober musicians might offer him a moment of clarity, but it ultimately did not help him achieve lasting sobriety. "Mike McCready and John Baker Saunders pulled Lane through those sessions, hoping that being around sober musicians would produce a moment of clarity, but it didn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Hiatus and Return
podcast.body: The band "went AWOL" after the height of grunge but has since returned, albeit with a new singer. "Alison Chains went AWOL and Sound Garden broke up. Meanwhile Pearl Jam went to great lengths to distance themselves from the whole grunge thing that they started."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Publishing Catalog Sale (N/A)
podcast.body: Alison Chains (likely Alice in Chains) are among the artists who have sold their music publishing catalogs as part of a trend since the mid-2010s. "Alison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rehab Attempts and Band Support
podcast.body: Layne Staley made several attempts at rehab, often in Los Angeles facilities, achieving brief periods of sobriety. At one point, all members of Alice in Chains flew to Los Angeles weekly to participate in his sessions, showing their support. "He enrolled in rehab several times, usually at a facility in Los Angeles, and each time he got sober for a bit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise of Grunge (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was instrumental in the emergence of grunge, which reshaped alt-rock into a genre centered on hard guitar rock, leading to increased record sales and widespread commercial success. "Thanks to Riff Ready Songs from Pearl Jam, Sound Garden, Alice in Chains and especially Nirvana, Alt Rock began to coalesce around hard guitar rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Robert Lang Studios Preference
podcast.body: Robert Lang Studios, located north of Seattle, was a favorite recording spot for Alice in Chains. This studio also holds significance for the Foo Fighters, as it was where their first record was made and where Nirvana recorded their last completed song. "Robert Lang Studios, a place north of the city that was a favorite spot for Alice and Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Seattle Grunge Origins and Dark Nature (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains emerged from Seattle in the early 1990s as one of the first and largest bands of the Grunge explosion. They were characterized by their "darkest" sound, heavily influenced by drugs, particularly heroin, which permeated both their music and the daily lives of the band members. "Allison Chains had been one of the first and one of the biggest bands to come out of Seattle during the Grunge explosion in the early 1990s, but they were also one of the darkest drugs, especially heroin, played a huge part not only the band's music, but in the day-to-day lives the guys in the group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Signed to Major Label
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was signed by Columbia Records, one of the major labels that began acquiring bands from the developing indie scene in Seattle. "Major record labels had heard about the developing indie scene and were in town snapping up some of the bigger bands. Allison Chains was signed by Columbia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: SoundScan Verification of #1 Records
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was among the alternative rock bands that ended up with "proper real number one records" due to the accurate sales data provided by SoundScan technology. This system confirmed the legitimate popularity and sales performance of their music. "And it's how Allison Chains and Sound Garden and Stone Temple Pilece and Pearl Jam all ended up with proper real number one records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Successful Niche in Grunge and Post-Grunge
podcast.body: The band carved out a "pretty good niche" within the Grunge and Post-Grunge music scenes, achieving significant sales and financial success. "Still Alison Chains had found a pretty good niche in the Grunge and Post-Grunge world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Susan Silver Becomes Sole Manager
podcast.body: When Kelly Curtis became fully engaged in managing Pearl Jam, he no longer had time for Alice in Chains, leading Susan Silver to become their sole manager. Silver maintains a close relationship with the band, describing them as "like brothers" to her, having shared extreme life experiences, both good and bad.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Temporary Sobriety after Kurt Cobain's Death
podcast.body: Layne Staley was temporarily "scared straight" by the death of Kurt Cobain, but he resumed drug use within weeks. "Lane was briefly scared straight by the death of Kurt Cobain, but within weeks he was back at it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Time Apart (4 years, 9 months, 18 days)
podcast.body: The band was effectively apart for this duration, measured from Layne Staley's death (April 19, 2002) to their first performance with new singer William DuVall (September 22, 2006). "So that's a break of four years, nine months, and 18 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Transition from Hair Metal
podcast.body: Alice in Chains transitioned from an earlier "quasi-hair metal" sound to a more "ragged" style, aligning with the evolving grunge movement. "A band called Allison Chains had moved from being quasi-hair metalers to something more ragged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unreached Potential Due to Drug Use
podcast.body: Alice in Chains was considered a "great band" with a "different and intriguing" sound and image. However, there is a "lingering feeling that they never reached their full potential" primarily because Layne Staley, and frankly the rest of the band, were heavily preoccupied with drug use. "Alison Chains, make no mistake about it, was a great band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: William DuVall Joins as Lead Vocalist
podcast.body: Following a successful show in March 2006, where William DuVall (singer for Comes with the Fall) performed as a guest vocalist, the band considered him for a permanent role. They had known and respected DuVall for five or six years. Other candidates, like Vinny Dombrowski of Sponge, were considered but didn't fit, and Scott Weiland was deemed unsuitable due to his drug issues. DuVall was chosen because he sounded close to Layne Staley without being a clone. His integration was gradual, leading to a full commitment by late 2008. "One of the guest vocalists that evening was a guy named William Duval, the singer with a group called Comes with the Fall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: William DuVall Joins as Singer
podcast.body: William DuVall, then singer for the Atlanta band Come With The Fall, had met Jerry Cantrell around 2000, and his band later opened for and functioned as Cantrell's backing band on solo tours around 2002. Their developing friendship led to DuVall becoming the new permanent singer for Alice in Chains. "Everybody became friends, talked to him to having DuVall be a permanent new singer for Alison Chains. And it happened."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Seattle Group Predating Grunge (1981) – First Client of Susan Silver
xref.body: The U-Men were a Seattle group that formed in 1981, predating the mainstream emergence of grunge by a few years. They were the first band managed by Susan Silver, who later became a prominent manager in the Seattle music scene for bands like Soundgarden and Alice in Chains. "Silver got her start managing the U-Men, a Seattle group that predated the whole Grunge thing by a couple of years in 1981."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Managed by Susan Silver (1983)
xref.body: Screaming Trees were an early client of Susan Silver, who started managing bands in Seattle in 1983 while still majoring in Chinese at the University of Washington. This management role predated her work with Soundgarden and Alice in Chains.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Marriage to Chris Cornell (September 1990) – Manager and Wife
xref.body: Susan Silver, who was already managing Soundgarden, began dating Chris Cornell and they married in September 1990. Their relationship lasted through significant periods in the rise of both Soundgarden and Alice in Chains, as well as Chris's early solo career and personal struggles. "She and Chris started dating, which probably had its awkward moments with the rest of the band, and then they got married in September of 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Missed Gig Due to Calendar Error (1991)
xref.body: In late November 1991, Jerry Cantrell went hunting, having promised to return for an important Alice in Chains gig on December 1st. He mistakenly believed that November had 31 days, leading him to miss the scheduled show. Upon his return on December 2nd (which he thought was December 1st), he was surprised to discover he had missed the performance. As a Christmas gift that year, his record label presented him with his very own pocket calendar. "Jerry honestly believed that November has 31 days and he ended up missing the gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Alice in Chains Opening Act Cancellation (1994)
xref.body: Alice in Chains, with Layne Staley, was scheduled to open for a Metallica tour in 1994 but had to bail due to Staley's severe drug addiction. "This included bailing as the opener for a Metallica tour in 1994."

xref.title: Band Breakup and Sean Kinney's Efforts (November 1997 - 2002)
xref.body: Alice in Chains officially broke up in November 1997 due to Layne Staley's inactivity as their frontman. Despite the breakup, drummer Sean Kinney regularly checked in on Staley, visiting his condo at least three times a week to ensure he was "okay," or as okay as circumstances allowed. Staley, however, was highly withdrawn, often ignoring calls and visitors at his door. "With nothing happening with their frontman, Allison Chains broke up in November 1997. Over the years that followed Lane deteriorated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Condo Purchase (1997)
xref.body: In April 1997, Layne Staley moved into a three-bedroom, 1500 square foot condo in Seattle's University District, purchased for $262,000. The property was bought by the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Alice in Chains Management Company, using "John LaRusta" as an alias to avoid his real name appearing on public records. "The purchaser was the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Allison Chains Management Company. John LaRusta was an alias used by Lane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Condo Purchase and Isolation (April 1997)
xref.body: In April 1997, Layne Staley moved into a three-bedroom, 1500 square foot condo in Seattle's University District, purchased for $262,000 by the LaRusta Trust, part of the Alice in Chains Management Company. Staley used "John LaRusta" as an alias to keep his real name out of public records. He spent his time painting, watching TV, playing video games, and doing "lots and lots of drugs." Alice in Chains guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit for him, which Staley used only occasionally, further highlighting his increasing isolation. "The purchaser was the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Allison Chains Management Company. John LaRusta was an alias used by Lane. He did one his real name used in any public records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Installation of Home Recording Outfit for Layne Staley (Post-1997)
xref.body: Jerry Cantrell, the guitarist for Alice in Chains, installed a home recording outfit in Layne Staley's condo. This was done after Staley moved into the condo in April 1997, providing him with the means to record music at home, although Staley only used it occasionally. "Allison Chains guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit that Lane used once in a while, but mostly he just painted, watched TV, played video games, and did drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Breakup Activities (1997-2002)
xref.body: After Alice in Chains broke up in November 1997 due to Layne Staley's inactivity, guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit in Layne's condo. However, Layne rarely used it, spending most of his time painting, watching TV, playing video games, and consuming "lots and lots of drugs." "With nothing happening with their frontman, Allison Chains broke up in November 1997."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Soundgarden Breakup (1997) – Tension from Manager/Wife Susan Silver and Separate Tour Transport
xref.body: The band broke up in 1997 partly due to the unresolvable conflict of interest created by Cornell being married to Susan Silver, who was also the band's manager (and the manager of Alice in Chains and Screaming Trees). By the end of the band's existence, each member was reportedly traveling separately by their own bus or plane between shows. After the divorce in 2002, Cornell filed a complaint with the California Labor Commission in 2006 alleging Silver had performed booking work without the required talent agent's license, and sought return of money she made from Soundgarden activities in 2005. "No conflict of interest there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery of Death (April 19, 2002)
xref.body: On April 17, 2002, Lane Staley's mother visited his apartment to inform him of Demri's brother's death, finding unopened mail and no answer at the door. Two days later, his accountants alerted Alice in Chains' former manager, Susan Silver, that no money had been withdrawn for two weeks, a significant red flag. Silver contacted Staley's mother, who returned to the condo, found his usually quiet cat, Sadie, meowing excessively, and then called 911. Police forced entry and discovered Staley's body amidst drug paraphernalia. "On April 19, the accountants who looked after Lane's money contacted Alison Chains former manager Susan Silver, saying that no money had been withdrawn from his bank account for two weeks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Friends' Efforts and Isolation (2002)
xref.body: In early 2002, despite attempts to record with Layne Staley, his singing voice was gone, and he had developed a lisp due to his missing teeth. Alice in Chains drummer Sean Kinney regularly checked Layne's condo online three times a week to ensure he was okay. Layne became extremely withdrawn, often ignoring calls and visitors at his door. His occasional outings consisted mainly of going to a local bar called The Rainbow, where he would sit in a back corner, drink, and pass out. "Allison Chains drummer Sean Kinney made sure that he checked in online at his condo at least three times a week just to make sure that everything was okay, or as okay as circumstances allowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Divorce from Chris Cornell (2004) – Followed by Lawsuit
xref.body: Susan Silver and Chris Cornell divorced in 2004, after a relationship that spanned the rise of Soundgarden and Alice in Chains, Soundgarden's breakup, Cornell's initial solo career, and his struggles with addiction, as well as the death of Alice in Chains singer Lane Staley. Their divorce was followed by a contentious lawsuit initiated by Cornell. "She and Chris divorced in 2004."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Anticipating the Grunge Explosion
xref.body: Despite their early presence, Mudhoney saw the grunge sound they pioneered explode into global prominence within two and a half years, largely thanks to bands like Soundgarden, Nirvana, Pearl Jam, and Alice in Chains, underscoring that they had accurately predicted the future of rock but were too early for widespread acceptance. "Imagine how Mudhoney must have felt to see a sound they'd play in here blow up without them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bridging Rock and Metal
xref.body: Silverchair was noted alongside Soundgarden, Nirvana, and Alice in Chains as bands that "slowly closed that big attitude gap between rock and old school metal" throughout the early and mid-90s, contributing to a more open musical landscape. "bands like Soundgarden and Silverchair Nirvana and the smashing pumpkins and Alice and Chains slowly closed that big attitude gap between rock and old school metal."

xref.title: Candidate for Alice in Chains Vocalist
xref.body: Vinny Dombrowski, from the Detroit band Sponge, was invited to rehearse with Alice in Chains as a potential replacement for Layne Staley but ultimately "didn't fit." "There was a guy named Vinny Dumbrowski from a Detroit band called Sponge. He was invited for rehearsals, but he didn't fit."

xref.title: Challenging Band Dynamics
xref.body: The band comprised Mike McCready (recovering alcoholic and drug addict), John Baker Saunders (who also had addiction issues), Layne Staley (Alice in Chains frontman, notorious drug addict), and Barrett Martin (Screaming Trees drummer, noted for his stability and academic background). Despite the varied personal struggles, the band managed to function. "Singing for the band was lain stately of Alice and Chains, a guy who had a reputation as being the biggest drug addict in a city of drug addicts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Co-Manager of Alice in Chains – Partnership with Kelly Curtis
xref.body: Susan Silver co-managed Alice in Chains with Kelly Curtis through their shared management company. When Mother Love Bone collapsed and transformed into Pearl Jam, Kelly Curtis shifted his focus to become Pearl Jam's full-time manager, leaving Susan to manage Alice in Chains independently. "When Mother Lovebone started to get hot, Kelly wanted to spend more time with them. Meanwhile, Ken wanted out, so Susan and Kelly became co-managers of Allison Chains through their own management company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Decent but Lesser Solo Work
xref.body: Jerry Cantrell has released "some decent solo records," but none have achieved the same level of impact or success as the collective accomplishments of Alice in Chains. "And a lot of some decent solo records, but nothing anywhere near the order of what Allyson accomplished together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Decline and Inability to Tour (Late 1990s)
xref.body: By the late 1990s, Layne Staley's health had deteriorated severely due to his drug addiction, rendering him unable to tour with Alice in Chains. He became a "hardcore, hermit junkie," having a network of dealers deliver a mix of smack, cocaine, and crack to his condo. "By the late 90s, Lane was in such rough shape that he couldn't tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

xref.title: Deteriorating Health and Isolation
xref.body: During his final years, Lane Staley's health worsened significantly; he suffered from unhealing open sores, and rumors circulated about him losing fingers or an arm due to abscesses. He became increasingly isolated from Alice in Chains and by 1999, rarely left his condo in Seattle's University District, where he primarily painted, played video games, watched TV, and used drugs delivered by dealers, only leaving to withdraw money from a bank machine for payments. "His drug use got much, much heavier. He did start seeing, or at least hanging out with, a woman named Michelle Crane. She spent as much time as she could with him, but his health kept getting worse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Fronted by Tina Bell, Bam Bam was a groundbreaking Seattle band that was "doing the grunge thing" in 1983, predating the genre's mainstream explosion by a couple of years. They performed before major grunge acts like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains gained prominence. "And they were doing the grunge thing in 1983, a couple of years before that sound really began to catch on."

His drug use intensified with the band's success, leading to countless failed attempts at sobriety in the mid-1990s and increasing isolation, especially after his girlfriend, Demri, died from drug-related complications. xref.title: Influence of Grunge on Rock
xref.body: Soundgarden was instrumental in bridging the "attitude gap" between rock and old-school metal throughout the early and mid-90s. Along with Nirvana and Alice in Chains, they openly cited bands like Black Sabbath, Judas Priest, and Kiss as "huge influences" on their music, contributing to a new open-mindedness in the rock scene. "Boys like Kurt Cobain and the dudes from Soundguard, Dinales and Chains weren't shy about saying, hey, don't diss black Sabbath and Judas Priest and kiss, they were pretty good bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Grunge Bands
xref.body: Black Sabbath was openly acknowledged by grunge musicians like Kurt Cobain and members of Soundgarden and Alice in Chains as a "pretty good band" and a "huge influence" on their music, demonstrating a re-evaluation and appreciation for old-school metal within the alternative scene of the 90s. "Boys like Kurt Cobain and the dudes from Soundguard, Dinales and Chains weren't shy about saying, hey, don't diss black Sabbath and Judas Priest and kiss, they were pretty good bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Grunge Bands
xref.body: Judas Priest was recognized by leading grunge figures such as Kurt Cobain and members of Soundgarden and Alice in Chains as a "pretty good band" and a "huge influence," indicating a breaking down of genre barriers and a newfound appreciation for traditional metal in the 90s alt-rock landscape. "Boys like Kurt Cobain and the dudes from Soundguard, Dinales and Chains weren't shy about saying, hey, don't diss black Sabbath and Judas Priest and kiss, they were pretty good bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Rock Music
xref.body: The Ramones are credited with profoundly influencing countless rock bands over several decades, with a direct lineage tracing back to their original version for bands like Rise Against, Metallica, Blink 182, Motorhead, Green Day, Guns N' Roses, The Clash, Sex Pistols, Rancid, The Pixies, The Beastie Boys, Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, The Strokes, The Offspring, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. "virtually any rock band of the last 25 years, 35 years, and you can draw a line back into the past, and that line will inevitably lead back to the Ramones."

xref.title: Pioneering Recording at Reciprocal Recording
xref.body: Bam Bam made their first record, the "Villains" EP, in 1984 at Reciprocal Recording. This made them the first Grunge band to record at that studio, which later became famous for hosting bands like Nirvana, Alice in Chains, Soundgarden, The Melvins, and Mudhoney. "They used reciprocal recording, making them the first Grunge band to make music there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pre-Death Decline and Drug Addiction
xref.body: Although he officially died in April 2002, Layne Staley "might as well have been dead long before that" due to the severity of his drug addiction. This addiction prevented Alice in Chains from realizing its full potential and led their record label to give up on expectations for new material. Most of his earnings were spent on drugs. "He didn't die until April 2002, but he really might as well have been dead long before that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

xref.title: Pre-dating Major Grunge Bands
xref.body: Bam Bam, with Tina Bell, was active and developing their sound before bands like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains. Their early contributions to the genre were not recognized in the same way as these later groups. "Tina and Bam Bam were doing their thing before Nirvana, before Soundgarden, before Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prisoner's Charity Work
xref.body: Wayne Kramer dedicated time to working with a prisoner's charity, collaborating with notable musicians such as Tom Morello, Billy Bragg, Perry Farrell, and Jerry Cantrell of Alice in Chains. "He also worked with a prisoner's charity alongside Tom Morello, Billy Bragg, Perry Farrell, and Jerry Cantrell of Ellison Chains."

xref.title: Regular Checks on Layne Staley (Years Leading to Death)
xref.body: Alice in Chains drummer Sean Kinney made a concerted effort to check on Layne Staley during his years of isolation and decline. Kinney would check in at Staley's condo at least three times a week, demonstrating a commitment to ensuring his bandmate was "okay, or as okay as circumstances allowed." However, Staley was often unresponsive to calls or knocks at his door. "Meanwhile, Allison Chains drummer Sean Kinney made sure that he checked in online at his condo at least three times a week, just to make sure that everything was okay, or as okay as circumstances allowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rise of Grunge (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Pearl Jam was a key band in the rise of grunge, which caused alt-rock to coalesce around hard guitar rock in the early 1990s, driving significant record sales and concert attendance. "Thanks to Riff Ready Songs from Pearl Jam, Sound Garden, Alice in Chains and especially Nirvana, Alt Rock began to coalesce around hard guitar rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rise of Grunge (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Soundgarden played a significant role in the rise of grunge, which led alt-rock to focus heavily on hard guitar rock in the early 1990s, attracting record labels and driving massive sales. "Thanks to Riff Ready Songs from Pearl Jam, Sound Garden, Alice in Chains and especially Nirvana, Alt Rock began to coalesce around hard guitar rock."

xref.title: Rise of Grunge (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Nirvana was especially influential in the rise of grunge, which caused alt-rock to coalesce around hard guitar rock, driving the genre to mainstream success and making it the dominant sound of alternative music. "Thanks to Riff Ready Songs from Pearl Jam, Sound Garden, Alice in Chains and especially Nirvana, Alt Rock began to coalesce around hard guitar rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Seattle Emo Sound
xref.body: Emerging from Seattle, Sunny Day Real Estate had little in common with the city's prominent grunge bands like Pearl Jam, Nirvana, Soundgarden, or Alice in Chains. They distinguished themselves with a slower, more melodic style, softly sung or crooned vocals (rather than screaming), and occasionally poppy elements. "Sunny day real estate had nothing in common with groups like Pearl Jam or Nirvana or Sound Guard and Aralus and Chains. They played slower than most other emo bands. Their songs were more melodic. And vocals tend to be softly sung or even crooned rather than screamed or shouted. In fact, some of the stuff that they did was downright poppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: William DuVall's Band
xref.body: William DuVall was the singer for the group Comes with the Fall when he was invited to be a guest vocalist for Alice in Chains in March 2006, eventually leading to him joining Alice in Chains full-time. "One of the guest vocalists that evening was a guy named William Duval, the singer with a group called Comes with the Fall."
